item.title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 3: CDC Over the Cluster Channel
item.description:
By the end of Part 2 ePHPm v0.7.0 ran exactly one SQLite engine, Turso, in process, for single-node and clustered mode alike. The sidecar was gone. What I skipped over is how a replica actually gets the primary’s writes, and what happens when the primary dies with data on it. That’s this post.

  • Part 1: Replication by sidecar with sqld
  • Part 2: Adding Turso
  • Part 3: CDC over the cluster channel (this post)

CDC from the engine itself

Turso has change data capture built in. Turn it on for a connection and every committed change lands in a turso_cdc table with a monotonically increasing change_id, the table, the rowid, and before/after images of the record. The primary tails that table and ships transaction batches. Replicas apply them. That’s the whole design, and it landed as an experimental path in #186 at the end of July, with the tailer and applier in litewire (litewire#10).

item.title: Calling Rust From PHP Without a Socket, Part 1: The Native Functions
item.description: ePHPm is a single Rust binary that embeds PHP, and it carries its own KV store and its own SQLite-backed database in the same process. For a long time the only way PHP code could reach that KV store was the same way it reaches Redis: open a TCP socket to the RESP listener ePHPm runs on localhost, encode a command, wait for the reply. That works, and every PHP Redis client in existence already speaks it, but it is a strange thing to do when the hash map you’re talking to lives a few pointers away in the same address space.

item.title: Zero-Dependency Deployments - Single Binary for WordPress
item.description: The standard way to run a WordPress site is four services: nginx for HTTP and TLS, php-fpm to run PHP, MySQL for data, and Redis once the site gets slow enough that someone installs an object cache plugin. That’s four processes, four config files, three sockets between them, and four things to upgrade. For a big site that’s fine. For a brochure site, a staging copy, a PR preview, a CI job that needs a real WordPress to test a plugin against, or a box at the edge, it’s absurd.

item.title: Security and Performance Hardening of a Rust Database Proxy
item.description:
litewire is the piece of ePHPm that lets PHP apps talk MySQL to a SQLite file. I wrote about how it works and about the MySQL quirks WordPress depends on. This one is the less visible half of August: an audit pass on litewire, a multi-tenant mode that turned a database proxy into a security boundary, and a performance regression I shipped and then had to go find.

It’s written in Rust, so memory safety is supposed to be the part I don’t have to think about. It mostly is. The use-after-free in this story was in a dependency, and the worst bug wasn’t a memory bug at all.

item.title: What Does One More WordPress Site Cost?
item.description: ePHPm v0.7.0 shipped per-site multi-tenancy: point [server] sites_dir at a directory, every Host maps to its own docroot and its own Turso database file, and one process serves all of them. The first question anybody asks about that is “how many sites fit on a box?”, and the honest way to answer it is to turn the question around. What does one more site cost? If you know the marginal RAM, file descriptors, CPU and disk for a tenant, the box size falls out of arithmetic.

item.title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 2: Adding Turso
item.description:
Part 1 ended with ePHPm running two SQLite engines: rusqlite in-process for a single node, and an embedded sqld child process for a cluster. The sidecar fell off a cliff past four concurrent writers and the best fix I could ship was a semaphore set to 1. This post is about replacing both engines with one, and about how I decided that engine was ready.

  • Part 1: Replication by sidecar with sqld
  • Part 2: Adding Turso (this post)
  • Part 3: CDC over the cluster channel

The thesis

Turso Database is a rewrite of SQLite in Rust, MIT licensed, file-format compatible, with MVCC for concurrent writers and change data capture built into the engine. Read that list again from the perspective of Part 1. An in-process engine means no child process and no Hrana hop. MVCC means writers don’t queue up behind one lock. Built-in CDC means the engine itself can tell me what changed, so ePHPm’s existing cluster layer can ship it. One engine for both modes, and clustered SQLite with zero child processes.

item.title: Faking MySQL's Quirks Well Enough to Fool WordPress
item.description: Last month I wrote about running SQLite behind a MySQL socket with litewire, and ended on “passing an install suite is not the same thing as behaving like MySQL”. That turned out to be accurate. On August 10th a few things happened at once: I put a real WordPress 7.0.3 site through a benchmark on ePHPm, A/B tested the new in-process database bridge against the wire path, and started building ephpm/db-wordpress, a wpdb drop-in that talks to the database in-process instead of over a socket. Between them they produced six litewire issues in about three hours. None of them broke the install. All of them made WordPress quietly do the wrong thing.

item.title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 1: Replication by Sidecar
item.description: Most PHP sites I have run in the last twenty years did not need a MySQL server. They needed a database, and MySQL was the one every framework spoke. With ePHPm I have been trying to get rid of that server for the common case, and the piece that makes it possible is litewire: PHP connects with plain pdo_mysql, litewire speaks the MySQL wire protocol, and the queries land in a SQLite file. WordPress and Laravel don’t know the difference. No mysqld, no child processes, just ephpm and a .db file.

item.title: SQLite as a Production Database via Protocol Translation
item.description: Most of the PHP sites I’d put on ePHPm don’t need a MySQL server. A brochure WordPress, an internal Laravel tool, a preview environment that lives for an afternoon. What they do need is something that looks like MySQL, because mysqli and pdo_mysql are the only database drivers their code has ever been pointed at. I mentioned this in the ePHPm pragmatism post as a one-paragraph “because”. This is the longer version, now that WordPress 7.0 and Laravel 13 both install and run end to end on it.
